not.text: The board doesn't regularly discuss, or get reports on, the security of the systems behind your essential functions.
When the board discusses security, it works from incomplete or outdated information, with no expert advice.
The board's direction doesn't effectively drive how those systems are secured in practice.
Senior managers or some teams think certain security policies don't apply to them, or expect exceptions.

achieved.text: The board owns your security approach and policy, and explains it meaningfully to risk decision-makers across the organisation.
The board regularly discusses security using timely, accurate information and expert advice.
One board member is accountable overall for security and keeps it regularly on the board's agenda.
The board's direction is turned into real working practices that control how systems are secured.
The board understands how system security supports your essential functions, and what a compromise would mean.
Security is seen as key to keeping essential functions running, and is part of every relevant discussion.

not.text: Key security roles are missing, vacant, or covered informally or only as and when needed.
People are given security duties without the authority or resources to carry them out.
Staff don't know what they are responsible for in keeping essential functions secure.

achieved.text: You have identified key security roles and responsibilities, and regularly review that they're still right.
Those roles are filled by capable, knowledgeable people with the time, authority and resources to do them.
It is clear who is accountable overall for the security of these systems.

not.text: Simple risk decisions keep getting passed up the chain, or never get made.
Local teams handle risks informally, or ignore them, when they should be reported through the formal risk process.
Decision-makers don't clearly know how much risk senior management will accept, beyond vague words like "cautious".
Decision-makers can't explain why they made their risk decisions.
Teams make risk decisions in silos, e.g. engineering and IT don't talk to each other about risk.
Risk ratings are too vague to prioritise, e.g. nearly everything is "medium" or "amber".

achieved.text: Senior management can see the key risk decisions being made across the organisation.
Decision-makers know they must make timely, effective risk decisions that stay within the level of risk senior management has said it will accept.
Risk decisions are handed down, or passed up, to whoever has the skills, knowledge, tools and authority to make them.
Past risk decisions are regularly reviewed to check they're still relevant and valid.

not.text: Risk assessments don't start from a clear, agreed view of who might attack you and what they could do.
Risk assessment results are too complex for decision-makers, and aren't communicated clearly or promptly.
Risk assessments are done once and never revisited, or not done at all.
Projects treat finishing a risk assessment as a box to tick, ignoring what it actually found.
There's no systematic process to make sure identified security risks are actually dealt with.
Systems are assessed on their own, ignoring how they rely on or connect to others, e.g. office IT and the operational technology (OT) that runs physical equipment.
Security controls are chosen at random or copied from a standard list, without asking how each one actually helps protect your essential functions.
Risks sit unresolved on the register for long periods, waiting for senior decisions or resources.

partial.text: You have a process that identifies, analyses, prioritises and manages security risks to essential functions.
Your risk assessments draw on an understanding of well-known threats and vulnerabilities in your systems.
Your risk process produces a clear set of security requirements that address the risks found.
Important findings from your risk process are shared with key security decision-makers and accountable people.
You reassess risk after significant changes, e.g. a system replacement, new technology or a change in threat.

achieved.text: You have a process that identifies, analyses, prioritises and manages security risks to essential functions.
Your risk thinking centres on how attackers could disrupt your essential functions, and how the way your systems are secured would help or hinder them.
Your risk assessments start from a clear view of who might attack you and how, kept up to date for your systems, your sector and national infrastructure more widely.
Your risk assessments draw on an understanding of the vulnerabilities in your systems.
Your risk process produces prioritised security requirements, each of which can be traced back to the risk it addresses.
Important findings from your risk process are shared with key security decision-makers and accountable people.
Your risk assessments are living documents, updated promptly when systems, their use, technology or threats change.
You regularly review how well your risk process works, and improve it as needed.
You look ahead to new technologies that attackers could use against your systems.

not.text: You're unable to work out who might attack your systems, how, and why.
You don't understand the threats to the systems behind your essential functions.
You don't have a clear, agreed view of who might attack you and what they could do.
You don't use what you know about threats when making risk decisions.

partial.text: You work out who might attack your systems and understand how common, everyday attacks would affect them.
You understand common types of cyber attack and how they might affect your systems, and keep this up to date.
You can predict what attackers might target in your systems to harm your essential functions.
Your understanding of threats is shaped by the kinds of incidents that commonly happen.
You use what you know about threats when making risk decisions.

achieved.text: You analyse in detail who might attack your systems and how, taking into account your sector and national infrastructure more widely.
You understand how capable, well-resourced attackers could systematically use their methods against your systems.
You look at your systems from an attacker's point of view and build realistic attack scenarios.
You understand the steps a capable, well-resourced attacker would need to take to reach their likely targets.
You identify, and can justify, measures that make it harder for an attacker to succeed at each step.
You keep a detailed, current understanding of threats, e.g. through threat intelligence and research.
You use your detailed understanding of threats when making risk decisions.
You have written down the steps for carrying out a detailed analysis of who might attack you and how.

not.text: A product or service is treated as a cure-all, and vendor claims are accepted without checking.
Security checks such as audits, tests or certifications are relied on without understanding what each one can and can't prove.
You assume security is fine because nothing has gone wrong yet.

achieved.text: You check that your security measures work, and keep working for as long as they're needed.
You know the different ways of gaining confidence in your security, such as testing, audits and certification, and pick the ones that suit your systems.
You can justify your confidence in security across technology, people and processes, and a third party could verify it.
Weaknesses found by these checks are assessed, prioritised and fixed promptly and effectively where needed.
You review how you check your security, to make sure those checks work and are still the best choice.

not.text: Your lists of relevant assets are incomplete, missing or lack detail.
Only some areas or types of asset are recorded and understood.
You don't understand how assets rely on each other, e.g. between office IT and the operational technology (OT) that runs physical equipment.
Information, including personal or critical data, is kept for long periods without a business need or retention policy.
Only one or two people hold knowledge critical to running or recovering your systems, with no succession plan.
Asset lists are neglected and out of date.

achieved.text: All relevant assets are identified and listed in suitable detail, and the list is kept up to date.
You recognise and record dependencies on supporting infrastructure, such as power and cooling.
You have ranked your assets by how important they are to running the systems behind your essential functions.
Every relevant asset, including physical ones, has someone responsible for managing it.
Assets are managed with security in mind throughout their life, from when they're created or bought to when they're retired or disposed of.

not.text: You don't know which of your data suppliers hold, or how they manage it.
Parts of your supply chain are subcontracted and you have little or no visibility of those subcontractors.
You don't know which contracts matter for security, or they lack proper security obligations.
Suppliers' access to your systems is unrestricted, unmonitored or bypasses your security controls.

partial.text: You understand the general risks suppliers may pose to your systems.
You know how far your supply chain extends, including subcontractors.
Suppliers can show their cyber security is at the right level to cope with common threats.
You know which contracts matter for security and include appropriate security obligations in them.
You know about every connection third parties have into your systems, and have evidence that each one meets your security requirements.
Your incident management plans cover incidents that might start in your supply chain.
You're confident suppliers protect information they hold that your systems need from common threats.

achieved.text: You deeply understand your supply chain, including subcontractors, and the wider risks it faces.
Your risk assessments and buying decisions weigh suppliers' ownership, nationality, partners, subcontractors and security approach.
Your supply chain risk planning considers capable, well-resourced attackers deliberately compromising your suppliers to get at you.
Your most important suppliers can show their cyber security is at the right level to withstand capable, well-resourced attackers.
You're confident suppliers protect information essential to your systems from capable, well-resourced attackers.
You know which contracts matter for security and include appropriate security obligations in them.
You actively manage relevant contracts, which may include a contract management plan.
Contracts set out which responsibilities belong to you and which to the supplier.
All network connections and data sharing with third parties are well managed, with controls that match the level of risk.
Where appropriate, you and your suppliers support each other in resolving incidents.

not.text: Your software suppliers don't know what their software contains or where its components came from.
Software, including updates and patches, gets little or no testing.
Updates and patches often cause new problems or don't fix existing ones.
Vulnerabilities are found in software that could easily have been prevented.

partial.text: Your software supplier follows secure development principles and practices.
Your software suppliers can show at least a basic understanding of what their software contains and where it came from.
Development, test and production environments, code and repositories are protected well enough to withstand common threats.
Testing uses a range of methods across the whole development process, checking both what the software does and qualities such as performance and security.
You've arranged to get timely security updates, patches and notifications from your software supplier.
You get software, updates and patches from suppliers in a way that stops them being intercepted or tampered with.
Your software suppliers have processes to find, report and fix security vulnerabilities.
Your software supplier will tell you about significant events that could harm your systems.
If you use open-source software, you've taken sensible steps, scaled to the risk, to become confident in its security and stay that way.
You have appropriate support and maintenance arrangements in place.

achieved.text: Your software suppliers follow a recognised secure development framework, such as NIST SSDF or Microsoft SDL.
Your supplier knows exactly what goes into its software, including third-party components, and watches those components for new vulnerabilities for the product's whole life.
Development, test and production environments, code and repositories are protected well enough to withstand capable, well-resourced attackers.
Software development is shaped by a current understanding of threats, using techniques like threat modelling (mapping out how someone might attack it) to find weaknesses.
You can confirm software, updates and patches are genuine and haven't been tampered with.

not.text: Your security policies and procedures are missing or leave gaps.
Your security policies and procedures aren't applied everywhere, or aren't applied consistently.
People often work around security policies and procedures to get their jobs done.
Your policies and procedures don't reflect how your organisation says it governs security and manages risk.
System security depends entirely on users carefully and consistently following manual steps.
Policies and procedures haven't been reviewed after major changes, such as new technology or regulations, or haven't been reviewed for too long.
Staff can't easily find your policies and procedures, or they're too detailed to remember or too hard to understand.

partial.text: Your policies and procedures set out your overall approach to governing security and managing risk, your technical security practices, and the regulations you must meet.
You review and update policies and procedures after major cyber security incidents.

achieved.text: You fully write down your overall approach to governing security and managing risk, your technical security practices, and the regulations you must meet.
Cyber security is built into all your policies and procedures, and measures of security performance are reported to executive management.
Your policies and procedures are practical, usable and suitable for reducing the risk of harm to the systems behind your essential functions.
Where policies and procedures depend on how people behave, they are practical, sensible and realistic to follow.
You review and update policies and procedures at suitably regular intervals to keep them relevant, not just after major incidents.
Any change to your essential functions, or to the threats they face, triggers a review of your policies and procedures.
Your systems are designed to stay secure even when people don't always follow security policies and procedures.

not.text: Policies and procedures are ignored or only partly followed.
People don't really understand how your policies and procedures help keep your essential functions running.
Staff don't know what your policies and procedures require of them.
You make no attempt to spot when policies and procedures are broken.
Your security policies and procedures don't fit together with the rest of your organisation's policies and procedures.
Your policies and procedures aren't communicated well across the organisation.

partial.text: Most policies and procedures are followed, and you monitor how they're applied.
Your security policies and procedures link up with your other policies, including HR checks on whether individuals can be trusted.
All staff know what your policies and procedures require of them.
Every breach that could harm your essential functions is fully investigated. Other breaches are tracked, checked for patterns and acted on.

achieved.text: All policies and procedures are followed, and you check both that they're applied correctly and that they actually improve security.
Your security policies and procedures link up with your other policies, including HR checks on whether individuals can be trusted.
Policies and procedures are communicated well at every level of the organisation, so staff clearly understand their responsibilities.
You act on every breach that could harm your essential functions, including lots of small breaches that add up to a bigger problem.

not.text: Your checks on who someone is, before giving them access, aren't thorough enough to be confident they are who they claim to be.
You can't identify each individual person or system that has access to the systems your essential functions rely on.
People or devices that shouldn't have access can get into the networks or systems your essential functions rely on.
More people and systems have access than your essential functions actually need.
How you check the identity of users, devices and systems when they log in doesn't follow current good practice.

partial.text: Before giving someone access, you check who they are thoroughly enough to be reasonably confident of their identity.
Every person and system with access is individually identified and has to prove who they are when logging in.
Only as many people and systems as your essential functions genuinely need have access.
Admin-level (privileged) access to all these systems needs a stronger login on top of a password, such as multi-factor authentication (MFA), e.g. a code from a phone app.
Every remote connection to these systems is individually checked: who it is, and what it's allowed to do.
You review the list of people and systems with access regularly, at least once a year.
How you check the identity of users, devices and systems when they log in follows current good practice.

achieved.text: Before giving someone access, you check who they are thoroughly enough to be highly confident of their identity.
Only approved people who have individually proved who they are can physically get to, or connect over the network to, the systems your essential functions rely on.
Only as many people and systems as your essential functions genuinely need have access.
All access to these systems, including remote access, needs a stronger login on top of a password, such as multi-factor authentication (MFA).
You review the list of people and systems with access regularly, at least every six months.
How you check the identity of users, devices and systems when they log in follows current good practice.

not.text: Users can connect to these systems from devices your organisation doesn't own and manage, such as personal phones or laptops.
People with admin rights can carry out admin tasks from devices your organisation doesn't own and manage.
You've done nothing to check the security of other organisations' devices or networks connected to your systems.
Plugging a device into your network gives it access without checking the device or the person using it.

partial.text: Only devices your organisation owns and manages can access the systems behind your essential functions.
All admin tasks are done from devices your organisation owns and manages, kept suitably separate from everyday user activity based on the risk.
Before other organisations' devices or networks can connect to your systems, you look into how secure they are and deal with any risks you find.
Simply plugging into a network socket or cable doesn't give access to any systems.
You can spot unknown devices being connected to your systems, and you investigate when it happens.

achieved.text: All admin tasks on these systems are done from highly trusted devices used for nothing else, such as Privileged Access Workstations.
Other organisations' devices or networks can only connect if independent experts have vouched for their security, or if they're dedicated solely to supporting your systems.
Devices prove who they are using digital certificates, and only known devices can access the systems your essential functions need.
You regularly scan for unknown devices and investigate anything you find.

not.text: You don't know, or don't manage, who has admin rights over these systems, including their infrastructure, platforms, software and settings.
Admin access to these systems relies on weak logins, such as a simple password alone.
The list of people with admin rights hasn't been reviewed recently, e.g. in the last 12 months.
Admin rights cover whole systems rather than being limited to what each person's role needs.
Admin access uses generic, shared or default accounts rather than accounts belonging to named individuals.
Terminals that stay logged in with admin powers, e.g. in a control room, have no extra controls, such as physical ones, limiting who can use them.
Nothing separates a person's different roles, e.g. the same account is used both for email and for admin tasks.

partial.text: All admin access to these systems needs a strong login, such as multi-factor authentication (MFA).
You know and manage exactly who has admin rights over these systems, including people from third parties.
Admin activity is routinely reviewed and checked, e.g. at least once a year.
People only get the specific admin rights they genuinely need for their job.

achieved.text: Admin work is done from separate accounts used only for that purpose, which are closely monitored and managed.
You can grant admin rights, and access for outside support providers, for a limited time only, after which they expire.
Admin rights are reviewed regularly and always updated when people join, change roles or leave.
All admin activity is routinely reviewed and checked, and recorded so it can be analysed or investigated later.

not.text: People are given more access than they need.
You don't check who a user, device or system is, or whether it actually needs access, before granting it.
People's access isn't reviewed when they change roles.
People's access still works after they've left your organisation.
The access that devices and systems have to each other isn't reviewed regularly, at least once a year.

partial.text: You follow a thorough process to confirm who each user is and give them only the access they need.
You regularly review who has access and remove access that's no longer needed.
People's access is reviewed when they change roles, as part of your process for people joining, moving and leaving.
All access by users, devices and systems is logged and monitored, but not cross-checked against other logs or access records.

achieved.text: You follow a thorough process to confirm who each user is and give them only the access they need, and you regularly audit that it's followed.
People's access is reviewed when they change roles, as part of your joining, moving and leaving process, and also at least once a year.
All access by users, devices and systems to the systems behind your essential functions is logged and monitored.
You regularly review access logs and cross-check them against other access records and the activity you'd expect to see.
Attempts by unapproved users, devices or systems to connect trigger an alert, and are quickly assessed and investigated.

not.text: You don't fully know what data your systems use and produce in running your essential functions.
You haven't worked out which data the systems behind your essential functions depend on.
You haven't worked out who can access your important data.
You haven't clearly set out what would happen if important data were compromised or became unavailable.

partial.text: You have found and recorded all data important to running these systems, plus any data that would help an attacker.
You have found and recorded who has access to that important data.
You regularly review where important data is kept, how it's sent, how much there is and how accurate it is.
You have identified every mobile device and portable storage item, such as USB drives, that holds important data.
You understand and write down how your essential functions would suffer if important data were wrongly accessed, leaked, changed or deleted, or became unavailable to the right people.
You occasionally check that those written impact assessments are still right.

achieved.text: You have found and recorded all data important to running these systems, plus any data that would help an attacker.
You have found and recorded who has access to that important data.
You always know where important data is kept, how much there is and how accurate it is.
You remove or reduce unnecessary copies of data, and old data you no longer need.
You have identified every mobile device and portable storage item that might hold important data.
You always know which network connections are used to send important data.
You understand how your important data fits into your operations, what its limitations are, and what it relies on.
You understand and write down how your essential functions would suffer if important data were wrongly accessed, leaked, changed or deleted, or became unavailable to the right people.
You check those written impact assessments regularly, at least once a year.

not.text: You don't know all your data connections, or which of them carry data important to your essential functions.
Important data travels over untrusted or public networks without technical protection, such as encryption.
Critical data routes that could fail, be jammed or get overloaded have no backup route.

partial.text: You have identified every connection that carries important data and protected each one effectively, in line with the risk.
You use physical or technical measures, e.g. encryption, to protect important data sent over untrusted or public networks, but have little or no confidence the protection is strong enough.

achieved.text: You have identified every connection that carries important data and protected each one effectively, in line with the risk.
You use physical or technical measures, e.g. encryption, to protect important data sent over untrusted or public networks, and can justify your confidence the protection is strong enough.
Where losing a data route would seriously affect your essential functions, e.g. through equipment failure or jamming, a suitable backup route is available.

not.text: You know little or nothing about where important data is stored.
Important stored data that's at risk hasn't been properly protected.
Backups are incomplete, untested, poorly secured, or might be out of reach when you need to recover from a disaster or keep the business running.

partial.text: You keep only the copies of important data that you need, and copies sent to less secure systems are cut down or read-only.
You use physical or technical measures to stop important stored data being accessed, changed or deleted without permission.
If you use encryption, you've set it up with suitable technical and procedural measures, but have little or no confidence it's strong enough.
You have suitable, secure backups so your systems can keep running if the original data is lost, e.g. offline or separate backups, or paper copies.

achieved.text: You keep only the copies of important data that you need, and copies sent to less secure systems are cut down or read-only.
You use physical or technical measures to stop important stored data being accessed, changed or deleted without permission.
If you use encryption, you've set it up with suitable technical and procedural measures, and can justify your confidence that it's strong enough.
You have suitable, secure backups so your systems can keep running if the original data is lost, e.g. offline or separate backups, or paper copies.
Old or archived data you still need is stored securely.

not.text: You don't know which mobile devices might hold important data.
You let important data be stored on devices your organisation doesn't manage, or that aren't managed to at least the same standard.
Data on mobile devices isn't technically protected, or only some of it is.

partial.text: You know which mobile devices hold important data.
Important data is only stored on mobile devices that meet at least the security standard set by your overall security policies.
Data on mobile devices is technically protected, e.g. encrypted.

achieved.text: Mobile devices holding important data are recorded, controlled by your organisation and set up following best practice for that type of device, with suitable rules in place.
You can remotely erase every mobile device that holds important data.
You keep as little important data on mobile devices as possible, and some may be deleted automatically after a set time.

not.text: Some or all devices, equipment or removable media holding important data are reused or thrown away without that data being securely erased.

partial.text: Important data is securely erased from all devices, equipment and removable media, such as USB drives, before they're reused or disposed of.

achieved.text: You record and track every device containing important data, whether it's a dedicated storage device or something with built-in storage.
Important data is securely erased from all devices, equipment and removable media before reuse or disposal, using an independently approved product or service.

not.text: The systems behind your essential functions aren't properly kept apart from your other systems.
People can browse the web or use email from the systems behind your essential functions.
Data moves between these systems and others in such complicated ways that it's hard to tell normal traffic from malicious traffic.
Remote or third-party connections bypass some network controls to get more direct access to these systems.

partial.text: You use people with the right expertise to design the systems behind your essential functions.
You build strong defences at the points where your systems connect to other organisations or the internet.
You keep the routes data takes between your systems and the outside world simple, so they're easy to monitor.
You design your systems so they're simple to recover.
Everything coming into these systems is checked at the network edge where possible; otherwise, extra monitoring watches for attacks hidden in files or messages.

achieved.text: You use people with the right expertise to design the systems behind your essential functions.
Your systems are split into security zones, with those behind your essential functions in a highly trusted, better-protected zone.
These systems are designed so data moves between their parts by simple routes, which makes security monitoring effective.
These systems are designed to be easy to recover.
Everything coming into these systems is protected against attacks hidden in files or messages, e.g. by converting, inspecting, cleaning and checking it.
If you use automated decision-making, such as AI, you set limits that stop it taking actions that could harm these systems.

not.text: You haven't worked out which assets need careful setting up to keep these systems secure.
Rules for installing and setting up operating systems securely aren't applied consistently across these systems.
System settings aren't recorded, or not in enough detail to rebuild the system or device.
Changes to security settings that affect your essential functions aren't recorded, or are recorded inconsistently.
Generic, shared, default and built-in accounts haven't been removed or switched off.
Ordinary users can change settings in ways that would weaken the security of these systems.

partial.text: You have identified and written down which assets need careful setting up to keep these systems secure.
Secure, standard set-ups are used for platforms and devices across your organisation.
Systems and devices of the same kind are set up consistently and securely, with only the features they need switched on.
Changes to security settings at the edges of these systems are approved and recorded.
Software is checked before anyone is allowed to install it.
Generic, shared, default and built-in accounts are removed or switched off, or their passwords changed where that's impossible. Accounts used by software and services are suitably protected.
Ordinary users can't change settings in ways that would weaken the security of these systems.

achieved.text: You have identified and written down which assets need careful setting up, and actively look after them, e.g. keeping settings secure and applying updates.
Every platform matches your defined secure standard set-up, or the latest version of its settings known to be good.
You closely control changes to your systems, making sure their settings stay secure and are recorded.
You regularly check that your systems still have the secure settings you expect.
Only approved software can be installed.
If you use automated decision-making, such as AI, you understand how it works and its decisions can be reproduced.
Generic, shared, default and built-in accounts are removed or switched off, or their passwords changed where that's impossible. Accounts used by software and services are suitably protected.

not.text: The systems behind your essential functions are run or maintained from devices your organisation doesn't own and manage.
You don't have good, up-to-date technical documentation for your systems.

partial.text: Only approved admins run or maintain these systems, using devices kept suitably separate from everyday user activity, based on the risk.
Technical information about your systems, such as documentation and network diagrams, is regularly reviewed and updated.
You prevent, detect and remove malicious software (malware) and unapproved software, using technical, procedural and physical measures as needed.

achieved.text: Only approved admins run or maintain these systems, using highly trusted devices used for nothing else, such as Privileged Access Workstations.
You regularly review and update technical information about your systems, such as documentation and network diagrams, and store it securely.
You prevent, detect and remove malicious software (malware) and unapproved software, using technical, procedural and physical measures as needed.

not.text: You don't know how exposed these systems are to publicly known security weaknesses.
You don't promptly fix or reduce weaknesses that can be reached from outside your organisation.
You haven't recently tested your systems to check what you think you know about their weaknesses.
You haven't taken suitable steps to protect systems or software that no longer get updates from their makers.
You aren't working towards replacing systems or software that no longer get updates.

partial.text: You keep an up-to-date picture of how exposed these systems are to publicly known security weaknesses.
You track and prioritise announced weaknesses in all the software you use, and promptly fix those reachable from outside, e.g. by patching.
Some weaknesses that can't be reached from outside are left with stop-gap protections for a long time.
You have stop-gap protections for unsupported systems and software while you work on moving to supported ones.
You regularly test your systems to fully understand their weaknesses.

achieved.text: You keep an up-to-date picture of how exposed these systems are to publicly known security weaknesses.
You track, prioritise and promptly fix announced weaknesses in all the software you use, e.g. by patching.
You regularly test your systems to fully understand their weaknesses, and have outside testers confirm what you've found.
You use, as far as possible, software, hardware and device firmware (the software built into equipment) that still gets updates from its makers.

not.text: You only partly understand everything needed to get these systems running again.
You haven't finished plans for keeping going and recovering from disaster, covering these systems and what they depend on.
You haven't fully checked whether your business continuity and disaster recovery plans would actually work in practice.

partial.text: You know every system and underlying technology needed to restore your essential functions, and how they depend on each other.
You know which order to recover systems in to restore your essential functions quickly and effectively.

achieved.text: Your continuity and disaster recovery plans have been tested to check they're practical, effective and complete, using suitable methods such as switch-over tests, discussion-based exercises or simulated attacks.
You use security news and threat intelligence to spot new or growing risks, and respond with immediate, possibly temporary, extra security measures, e.g. during a damaging malware outbreak.

not.text: The systems behind your essential functions aren't properly kept apart from other systems.
People can browse the web or use email from the systems behind your essential functions.
You don't understand, or have no plans to deal with, all the capacity limits and single points of failure that could disrupt your essential functions.

partial.text: These systems are kept separate from your business systems by network controls rather than physically, e.g. in their own zone (a DMZ) on the same network.
People can't browse the web or use email from the systems behind your essential functions.
You've identified capacity limits and single points of failure, such as limited bandwidth or a single network route, but haven't fully dealt with them.

achieved.text: These systems are separated from other business and external systems by technical and physical means, e.g. their own network, infrastructure and user administration.
People can't browse the web or use email from the systems behind your essential functions.
You've identified and dealt with all capacity limits and single points of failure, such as limited bandwidth or a single network route.
You've identified and dealt with location-based weaknesses, e.g. copying key systems to another site and having alternative physical routes and providers for important connections.
You review and update your assessments of dependencies, capacity and location weaknesses, and how you've dealt with them, when needed.

not.text: Your backups don't cover all the data and information needed to restore your essential functions.
You don't back up often enough to restore your essential functions effectively.
Your restore process doesn't bring your essential functions back quickly enough.

partial.text: You have suitably secured backups, covering data, settings, software, equipment, processes and knowledge, that you could still reach after a major event such as a ransomware attack.
You routinely test your backups to make sure the backup process works and the backups can actually be used.

achieved.text: Your thorough, automatic and tested backups, covering both systems and procedures, are kept securely at central or secondary sites so you can recover from a major event.
Backups of all important data and information needed to recover your essential functions are made, tested, written up and regularly reviewed.

not.text: People don't understand what part they play in keeping the systems behind your essential functions secure.
People don't know how to raise a cyber security concern.
People think reporting problems might get them into trouble.
Staff see your approach to security as getting in the way of the business, which may push them into bad security habits.
Formal or informal incentives and rewards work against good security.

partial.text: Executive management understand, and widely share, why a positive security culture matters, and you've described the attitudes and behaviours you expect.
Everyone in your organisation understands what part they play in keeping these systems secure.
Everyone knows who to contact and where to find more information about cyber security, and how to raise an issue.
You find and fix the things that stop people behaving in the secure ways you want.

achieved.text: Executive management clearly communicate the organisation's security priorities and goals to all staff, and your organisation shows positive security attitudes and behaviours.
People who raise possible security incidents or issues are treated positively.
People at every level routinely report security concerns and are recognised for helping keep the organisation secure.
Management are visibly committed to, and actively involved in, cyber security.
Your organisation talks openly about cyber security and takes every concern seriously.
People across the organisation work together on security, bringing their own expertise and sharing ownership of it.

not.text: Some teams that run or support your essential functions have had no cyber security training at all.
Only certain roles get cyber security training.
Your records of who has had cyber security training are missing or incomplete.
Training is treated as the answer to every user security problem.
Training success is judged only by how many people completed it, not by whether it actually improved security behaviour.
Training materials are out of date, contradict themselves, or conflict with other policies and procedures.

partial.text: You've defined suitable security training and awareness for every role, from executives to the most junior staff.
You use a range of teaching and communication methods so security training and awareness reach as many people as possible.
Cyber security information is easy to find.

achieved.text: Everyone, from the most senior to the most junior, follows a suitable cyber security training path.
Each person's security training is tracked and refreshed at suitable intervals.
You routinely check that your security training and awareness activities reach as many people as possible and actually work.
Security information and good-practice guidance is easy to find and widely available, and you know people actually use it.

not.text: You don't collect information about the security and running of the systems behind your essential functions.
You can't check back on what users and systems have done on these systems.
You don't monitor traffic going in and out of your network.
Your logs can't be lined up against one accurate, shared clock.
Logs are kept where the people and systems allowed to use them can't easily get to them.
Your monitoring tools can't be set up to use new sources of log data as they're added.
Your monitoring tools can only use a small part of the log data you collect.
You don't know where log data is kept or how long it should be kept for.
You have no way of making sure logs are being recorded as expected and are there when you need them.

partial.text: You collect security and operational information from some parts of these systems, but not all.
You monitor some user and system activity, but not against a fully agreed list of suspicious or unwanted behaviour.
You monitor traffic going in and out of your network, recording at least which network addresses (IP addresses) connect to which.
Some, but not all, of your logs can be easily searched to help with investigations.
Your monitoring tools work with most of your log data, with some setting up.
Your monitoring tools can use log data that would reveal all common threats.
You make sure log data is available for analysis when it's needed.

achieved.text: Your monitoring is based on a thorough understanding of your systems, how attackers operate, and what you need to record and watch to spot incidents affecting your essential functions.
Your monitoring data has enough detail to spot security events and incidents quickly and reliably, and to support investigations. You review this regularly and after major events.
Extensive monitoring of user and system activity lets you quickly spot rule-breaking, suspicious behaviour, or anything out of the ordinary that could signal an attack.
You monitor both individual computers and devices, and the network traffic between them.
Every new system behind your essential functions is considered as a possible source of monitoring data, so your coverage stays complete.
Your logs are lined up against an accurate, shared clock, so events in different logs can be matched up.
You add extra information from other systems to your log data to build a fuller picture of what's happening.
Your monitoring tools use log data to pinpoint exactly what activity happened.
You regularly review the sources and tools you use for logging and monitoring to make sure they still work well.

not.text: Unauthorised people, systems or attackers could easily edit or delete log data.
Nothing controls which users and systems can get at log data.
Nobody watches who accesses log data.
You have no policies on who can access log data.

partial.text: Only approved users and systems can access log data.
There's some monitoring of access to log data, e.g. copying, deleting, changing or even viewing it.
You've decided how long to keep log data, and you stick to it.
Your policies set out the legitimate reasons for accessing log data.

achieved.text: Access to log data is limited to the users and systems that need it for their work.
Your logging set-up is protected against the same kinds of threat it's designed to spot, covering both the system itself and the data in it.
Log data is only analysed or reformatted using copies, so the original stays untouched.
Every action on log data, e.g. copying, deleting, changing or even viewing it, can be traced to a specific user or system.
Log data is protected from tampering and checked, and any change or deletion is detected and traced to whoever made it.

not.text: You don't promptly apply updates to your detection tools once received, e.g. new antivirus signatures or indicators of compromise (known signs of an attack).
Security alerts about these systems aren't prioritised.
You can't add extra context to security alerts from these systems.
You can't reliably spot known signs of an attack on these systems, such as traffic from an attacker remotely controlling a machine, e.g. because your logs lack detail.
You don't watch for unusual user or system behaviour that could signal an attack.
Logs are rarely checked.

partial.text: You easily spot known signs of an attack (indicators of compromise) on these systems, such as traffic from an attacker remotely controlling a machine.
You apply some updates, new signatures and indicators of compromise promptly.
Security alerts about these systems are prioritised.
You add extra context to alerts from these systems, but separately rather than as part of the original alert.
Detection and alerting rely on standard tools used without customisation, or on users reporting things.
Everyone who supports your essential function has a written, shared process for reporting events and possible security incidents.
Where appropriate, detections automatically trigger action, e.g. antivirus quarantining malware it finds.
You check for unusual user or system behaviour that could signal an attack, but not regularly.
Logs are checked at regular intervals.

achieved.text: You easily spot known signs of an attack, such as an attacker remotely controlling a machine, as well as unusual behaviour that could signal an attack.
You apply all updates, new signatures and indicators of compromise promptly.
Security alerts about all these systems are prioritised, and this is used to help manage incidents.
Alerts routinely have extra context added, almost in real time, as part of the original alert.
Alerts and the rules behind them are regularly reviewed and tested so they fire quickly and reliably, and real incidents can be told apart from false alarms.
Alerts and the rules behind them can be customised and fine-tuned to cut false alarms and improve responses.
Detection and alerting may use both standard, off-the-shelf tools and rules, and your own custom ones.
You constantly watch for unusual user and system behaviour that could signal an attack, and raise alerts based on what you find.
Logs are monitored constantly, almost in real time.

not.text: You don't assess and sort (triage) alerts from your security detection tools, e.g. antivirus or intrusion detection systems.
You don't sort alerts and incidents by type and by priority or severity.
You have no step-by-step guides (playbooks) to follow when assessing alerts.
You don't keep records of how alerts were assessed.
You don't understand normal user or system behaviour well enough to make good decisions when assessing alerts.

partial.text: You investigate and assess alerts from some of your security tools, and act on them.
You have step-by-step guides (playbooks) for the most common situations, which people use when appropriate and which are regularly reviewed to keep them effective.
You assess some alerts, and record the actions taken by your monitoring staff.
You sort alerts and incidents by type and by priority or severity.
Your understanding of normal user or system behaviour helps you make decisions when assessing alerts.

achieved.text: You investigate and assess alerts from all of your security tools, and act on them.
You have step-by-step guides (playbooks) for every realistic situation, which people use when appropriate and which are regularly reviewed to keep them effective.
You sort alerts and incidents by type and by priority or severity.
You record everything your monitoring staff do when assessing alerts, and use these records to drive improvements.
Assessing alerts gives enough information to prioritise what happens next, e.g. containing damaging malware.
You understand normal user and system behaviour, and threats, well enough to make good decisions when assessing alerts.

not.text: Nobody is responsible for monitoring and detecting security issues.
Your monitoring staff lack the right specialist skills.
Your monitoring staff can't report in the way your governance requires.
Monitoring staff don't know what essential functions you provide or which assets support them, so can't judge how important logs and events are.
Monitoring staff know nothing about other roles or tasks, outside security monitoring, that matter to running your essential functions.
Monitoring staff are so swamped by data and alerts that they've stopped giving each one proper attention.

partial.text: Monitoring staff have some investigation skills and a basic understanding of the data they work with.
Monitoring staff can report to other parts of the organisation, e.g. security directors or resilience managers.
Monitoring staff can follow most of the required processes.
Monitoring staff know about some of your systems and essential functions, and can handle alerts relating to them.
Monitoring staff have some understanding of how your organisation operates, its people, processes and systems, which helps them monitor better.
Monitoring staff handle their workload and cases effectively.

achieved.text: Named monitoring staff are responsible for analysing, investigating and reporting on alerts, both proactively and in response, covering security and performance.
Monitoring staff have defined roles and skills covering every part of the monitoring and investigation process.
Monitoring staff follow policies and procedures that meet all internal and external governance reporting requirements.
Monitoring staff are free to go beyond the set process to investigate unusual threats.
Monitoring staff know your systems, essential functions and related assets, and can spot and prioritise alerts and investigations relating to them.
Monitoring staff help decide what new log data to collect, and make good use of it.
Monitoring staff can follow all of the required processes.
Monitoring staff understand how your organisation operates, its people, processes and systems, well enough to make monitoring more effective.
Monitoring staff handle their workload and cases effectively, and spot ways to improve.

not.text: You have no sources of information about current threats (threat intelligence).
You don't assess how useful your threat intelligence is, or give feedback to its providers or other users.
You don't know what's needed to make the most of threat intelligence in your monitoring.
Your threat intelligence is unreliable, or the right people and systems don't act on it promptly.
You have no settled idea of what unusual activity to look for that might signal an attack.
You don't get updates for all your detection tools, e.g. antivirus or intrusion detection systems.
You don't understand normal user and system behaviour well enough to spot attacks by noticing what's unusual.

partial.text: You know how effective your threat intelligence is, e.g. by tracking how it helps you identify incidents.
You may use threat intelligence services, but don't necessarily choose them based on your business needs or the specific threats in your sector.
You treat unusual behaviour seen in past attacks, on your own or others' systems, and in threat intelligence, as warning signs.
You get regular updates for all your detection tools, e.g. antivirus or intrusion detection systems.

achieved.text: You track how effective your threat intelligence is, and actively share feedback on how useful it was with others, e.g. sector partners, providers and government agencies.
Any threat intelligence feeds you use were chosen based on the risks and threats facing your business and sector.
You get relevant, reliable threat intelligence that can be acted on to the right people and systems promptly.
You put threat intelligence into context, linking it to why and how attacks happen, to guide your monitoring.
You know normal user and system behaviour so well that looking for anything unusual is an effective way to spot attacks, e.g. you know which systems should communicate, and when.
The unusual behaviour you watch for is based on the kinds of attack most likely to affect the systems behind your essential functions.
The warning signs you watch for are regularly updated to reflect changes to your systems and the latest threat intelligence.
You're able to share threat intelligence, e.g. effective ways to detect attackers, with sector partners, providers and government agencies when needed.

not.text: You don't know what resources you'd need to actively search for attackers your monitoring has missed (threat hunting).
You don't have access to an effective threat hunting capability.
Your threat hunts have no structure, and little or nothing is written down.

partial.text: You know what resources you need for threat hunting and can deploy them promptly, on an occasional basis.
You carry out effective threat hunting, but not often enough for the risks your systems face, e.g. only after a tip-off from a trusted source.
Your threat hunts follow set, written methods, e.g. starting from a theory, from data, or from a specific user or device, to find attacks automated tools miss.
You write up the details of each threat hunt and what you found afterwards.

achieved.text: You understand what resources threat hunting needs, and it's part of your normal, day-to-day work.
You hunt for threats as often as the risks to your systems require.
Your threat hunts follow set, written methods, e.g. starting from a theory, from data, or from a specific user or device, to find attacks automated tools miss.
Where it makes sense, you turn what you learn from threat hunts into automated detections and alerts.
You routinely record details of past threat hunts and follow-up work, and use them to improve your hunting and overall security.
You can justify your confidence that your threat hunts work, and you review and update the process to match the risks your systems face.
Where it makes sense, you use automation to improve threat hunts, e.g. automating some stages.
Your threat hunts focus on how attackers behave and operate, rather than on single clues such as file fingerprints (hashes), IP addresses or domain names.

not.text: Your incident response plan isn't written down.
Your incident response plan doesn't cover the essential functions your organisation has identified.
Relevant staff don't understand your incident response plan well.

partial.text: Your incident response plan covers the systems behind your essential functions.
Your incident response plan thoroughly covers scenarios, but only the likely effects of known, well-understood attacks.
Everyone involved in responding to incidents understands your incident response plan.
Your incident response plan is written down and shared with everyone who needs it.
Your incident response plan is easy to get to, even if an incident has knocked out your IT systems.
Your incident response plan is regularly reviewed to keep it effective.

achieved.text: Your incident response plan is based on a clear understanding of the security risks to the systems behind your essential functions.
Your incident response plan is complete, covering an incident from start to finish, roles and reporting, and both known types of attack and new, never-seen ones.
Your incident response plan is written down and joined up with wider business plans, suppliers' response plans, and supporting services such as power and cooling.
The parts of the business involved in running your essential functions have been told about, and understand, your incident response plan.

not.text: You haven't arranged for the right resources to be available to carry out your response plan.
Your response team aren't equipped to make good response decisions and act on them.
You lack adequate fallback arrangements to keep your essential functions running during an incident.

achieved.text: You know what resources you'll probably need to respond to an incident, and have arranged for them to be available.
You know what information you'll probably need to make response decisions, and have arranged for it to be available.
Your response team have the skills and knowledge to decide what's needed to limit harm, and the authority to do it.
Key roles have backup people, and everyone involved in running and recovering your essential functions shares the know-how to deliver them.
Fallback arrangements can be quickly switched on to keep your essential functions running, perhaps at a reduced level, if your main systems fail.
You've arranged extra outside help for incident response if needed, e.g. specialist cyber incident responders.

not.text: Exercises only test one part of the process, e.g. that backups work, rather than all areas.
Incident response exercises aren't held routinely, or only happen now and then without a plan.
What you learn from exercises isn't fed into your organisation's lessons-learned process.
Exercises don't test every stage of your response.

achieved.text: Exercise scenarios are based on real incidents at your own or other organisations, or built from experience or threat intelligence.
Exercise scenarios are written down, regularly reviewed and checked for realism.
Exercises are held routinely, and the findings are written up and used to improve your response plans and security.
Exercises test every stage of your response for your essential functions, including getting back to normal service.

not.text: You usually can't trace incidents back to their underlying cause, or see what contributed to them across your wider systems.
You have no formal process for investigating what caused an incident.
Investigators settle on a theory early and only look for evidence that supports it.
Investigations focus only on finding someone to blame.

achieved.text: You routinely analyse incidents afterwards as a key part of learning lessons from them.
Your analysis is thorough, covering organisational factors such as policies, technical factors such as system design, human factors such as training, and changes in threat.
The analysis team gets all the relevant incident data it needs.
Your analysis considers what could have happened in realistic alternative circumstances, e.g. "what if" or "if only" scenarios.

not.text: After incidents, lessons aren't captured, or only a narrow set are.
Improvements identified after an incident aren't made, or aren't given enough priority.
Changes are rushed in as a knee-jerk reaction to an incident, without proper analysis and testing to check they're right.
You wait for a serious or high-profile incident before taking steps to improve.

achieved.text: You have a written incident review process that makes sure lessons from every incident, including near misses, are identified, recorded and acted on.
Lessons learned cover reporting, roles, governance, skills and policies, not just the technical side of your systems.
You use lessons learned to improve security, including updating and retesting response plans when needed.
Security improvements from lessons learned are prioritised, and the most important are completed promptly.
Findings go to senior management and feed into risk management and ongoing improvement.
You get the most from lessons learned by exploring "what if" and "if only" scenarios.
You learn from incidents reported elsewhere in your sector and across national infrastructure more widely.
